pl-l2d33c2-d1e108.summary: Cites the Enchiridion: many sins can be understood in Adam's one transgression if divided into members: pride, loving his own rather than God's power; sacrilege, not believing God; homicide, casting himself into death; spiritual fornication, his mind's integrity corrupted by the serpent; theft, taking forbidden food; avarice, desiring more than should suffice.
claims: Adam's one sin contains many sins.

pl-l2d33c2-d1e111.summary: Cites Augustine discussing by opinion rather than assertion: it is not improbably said that infants are bound by their parents' sins as well as the first humans', since 'I will render the sins of fathers upon the sons' holds them before regeneration; David speaks of iniquities and sins because there are many sins in the one that passed to all, and other parental sins, which cannot so change nature, bind children by guilt unless grace helps.
claims: Augustine offers the view as not improbable.

pl-l2d33c2-d1e114.summary: Continues Augustine: it can be debated whether one is entangled in the sins of all ancestors from Adam, so that the later one is born the worse, or whether God limits his wrath to the third and fourth generation in mercy, lest the unregenerate be crushed in damnation; whether anything else can be found from Scripture he dares not rashly affirm.

pl-l2d33c2-d1e120.summary: Concludes that Augustine said these things not asserting but reporting various opinions.

pl-l2d33c2-d1e123.summary: Argues that otherwise Augustine would contradict himself, since in the same book he says the punishment of those who have only original sin is the mildest of all, and others' damnation is more tolerable the less their iniquity.

pl-l2d33c2-d1e126.summary: Concludes that infants are bound by no ancestors' sins but Adam's; if punished for parents' actual sins as well as original sin, they would be punished as much or more than their parents. They will be damned only for original sin, feeling no material fire or worm of conscience, only lack of God's vision forever. So infants are bound by one sin, not many.
claims: Infants are bound only by original sin.
Their punishment is lack of the vision of God.

pl-l2d33c2-d1e129.summary: Gives Augustine's resolution of the plurals: Scripture often uses singular for plural ('take away the serpent') and plural for singular ('they are dead who sought the child's life' of Herod; 'they made gods of gold' of one calf); so the one original sin is signified by plurals in 'remission of sins' and 'conceived in iniquities.'
claims: Plurals can signify the one original sin.

pl-l2d33c2.summary: Augustine says many sins can be seen in Adam's one transgression: pride, sacrilege, homicide, spiritual fornication, theft, avarice. He discusses ancestral sins by opinion rather than assertion, saying it is not improbable that infants are bound by their own parents' sins, but leaving open whether all ancestors' sins are contracted or God limits his wrath to four generations. Lombard holds Augustine was reporting opinions, since he also says unbaptized infants with only original sin have the mildest punishment of all, which would be impossible if they bore their ancestors' actual sins. So infants are bound by one sin only, original sin, and suffer no fire or worm of conscience, only perpetual lack of the vision of God. Scripture's plurals stand for a singular, as 'serpent' for serpents and 'gods' for one calf.
claims: Many sins can be distinguished in Adam's one transgression.
Augustine discussed ancestral sins as opinion, not assertion.
Infants with original sin alone receive the mildest punishment.
Infants are bound only by original sin, not by ancestors' actual sins.
Unbaptized infants suffer no fire or worm of conscience, only lack of the vision of God.
Scripture's plurals for original sin stand for a singular.
